idea: Teach 2nd graders to build a paper airplane and measure flight distance, one 30-minute session.

assessment.summary: A 30-minute 2nd-grade paper airplane build-and-measure session is safe, cheap, and age-appropriate, but as written it reads as a single fixed build with one measurement — it needs a design-variable comparison to create real decision points and productive struggle.

grade_level_fit.notes: Grade band explicitly stated (2nd grade, ~7-8 years old). Folding a simple dart glider, throwing it, and measuring distance with a tape or floor markers is well within 2nd-grade motor and numeracy ability, especially if measurement is scaffolded (whole feet, floor tape marks, or non-standard units like tile counts).

materials_feasibility.notes: Requires only copy paper, tape, markers, and a measuring tape or pre-marked floor — items any afterschool program already has. No sourcing risk.

instructor_capability.notes: No domain expertise needed. A non-specialist can teach a fold sequence and run a measure-and-record loop with minimal prep; the only prep is practicing the fold and pre-marking a throwing lane.

ai_assistance_value.notes: Claude can author fold-step visuals/scripts, a 2nd-grade-friendly data recording sheet, guiding questions about lift and drag in plain language, prediction prompts, and a short wrap-up discussion — plenty of authorable material even though the activity is physical.

time_scope_fit.notes: Fits a single session, but 30 minutes is tight for 2nd graders: fold instruction alone typically runs 10-12 minutes with hands-on help. Scope must be capped at roughly one fold design plus one modification and about 3 throws each, or the measurement/discussion phase will get cut.

safety.notes: Minimal risk. Standard mitigations only: designated one-direction throwing lane, no throwing at faces, students stand behind a line while others throw, and no sharp folding tools or paper-edge hazards beyond normal classroom paper handling.

pedagogical_alignment.notes: As stated, students follow one fold recipe and record one number — there is no design decision, no variable to test, and no iteration, so there is nothing to struggle productively with. The measurement becomes a demonstration rather than an experiment.

open_questions: Is there an open throwing lane of at least ~20-25 feet (hallway, gym, or cleared classroom) available for the session, and can it be pre-marked for measurement?
What is the expected class size and is there a second adult/volunteer? Fold help for 2nd graders is hands-on and drives whether 30 minutes is realistic.
Should measurement use standard units (feet/meters with a tape) or non-standard units (floor tiles, footsteps) to match where this group is in their math sequence?
suggested_changes: Add one controlled design variable so students make a decision and compare results — e.g. every student folds the same base plane, then chooses ONE change (add a paperclip nose weight, bend up the wing tips, or widen the wings) and measures before vs. after.
Structure the session as predict -> throw 3 times -> record -> modify -> re-throw, so students have data to reason about rather than a single number.
Pre-crease or pre-print fold lines on the paper to reclaim 5+ minutes of instruction time, keeping the 30-minute session viable with the added test-and-compare phase.
Cap the recording sheet to three throws before and three after, with a simple 'farthest throw' comparison, so data handling stays inside 2nd-grade numeracy.
